column2: A large-caliber bullet struck him head-on. He staggered back two steps and fell on his back.
A casing spun from the sniper rifle and hit the ground. Lu Mingfei blew across its chamber, his face vacant, expressionless.
Chu slowly turned, golden pupils reflecting Murasame’s gleam. He dropped the sword and raised both hands. “Who are you?”
Chu Zihang. It really was his high school’s legend, the Chu Zihang someone like Lu Mingfei could only watch from afar.

When Lu Mingfei was a freshman, Chu had been Student Council president, inspecting each class and awarding scores during morning exercises. Even in light rain, they had to keep going. Above them, dressed in spotless white, Chu would pass slowly along the top-floor corridor, looking down. Their movements were perfectly synchronized, like toy soldiers’.
But his eyes hadn’t been this dazzling gold then.
“Lu… Mingfei?” Miraculously, Chu spoke his name.
Once, that would have moved him beyond words. The legendary senior remembered his name, perhaps had even noticed him. He wasn’t one of Chu’s lovestruck fangirls, but it was an honor all the same.
Now he said nothing, only watched Chu coldly.
“The game’s over. I can concede!” Chu felt murderous intent cutting toward him against the wind and decided to surrender.

The black muzzle rose again. Lu Mingfei’s bones moved with mechanical precision. He worked the action. A round slid into place. His finger tightened on the trigger. The gun’s mechanisms seemed to merge with his skeleton. Muzzle aligned, his bones locked into their proper positions one by one. Chu’s figure appeared in the sights.
“Dis…” Lu Mingfei uttered the syllable coldly.
The thunderous gunshot swallowed the next.
He pulled the trigger. The bullet screamed from the barrel and pierced Chu’s chest. An enormous blossom of blood burst outward.

The campus fell silent. Sunlight shone on the gun smoke, turning it a lovely gold. Lu Mingfei seemed to stand in morning mist. After a long time, he propped the rifle against a wall, sat slowly on the steps, and rested his forehead on his clasped hands.
A vigorous march rang across campus. The long-silent PA system seemed to have woken from a nap.
He started, as if waking from a dream. Looking at the bodies, he raised his hands, but didn’t know whom to surrender to.

An unfamiliar building’s doors opened, and doctors and nurses poured out with cases bearing the college emblem. Dazed, he watched doctors inject the corpses, afraid to speak. A small old man with a shining bald head and thin, round gold-rimmed glasses approached, holding a handkerchief over his nose and mouth, frowning and sighing. The bullet-pocked walls made his sighs more heartfelt. Apparently, he cared less about the death toll than the property damage.
He looked Lu Mingfei up and down. “A freshman, judging by your clothes?”
Lu Mingfei nodded.

“Professor Manstein! Disciplinary Committee!” The little old man looked contemptuous. “Sit somewhere out of the way! Students these days! Instead of putting studies first when you arrive, you join these pointless games! Is it fun? Is it?” Growing angry again, he pointed at the cratered granite walls. “Money! All of that is money!”

Lu Mingfei shifted to one side. Someone patted his shoulder from behind. “Don’t mind him. Manstein’s a good friend. A little too fond of money, that’s all. I’ll ask him to look after your coursework.”
He nodded quickly. “Yes, yes… But what exactly…”
He turned and froze. It was Professor Guderian, whose chest had been blown open. The old man still bore a huge bloodstain, but looked wonderfully spirited.
“A ghost!” was his first reaction.
“Alive! I’m alive!” The professor waved hastily. “Feel me. I’m warm!”
“So… you’ve successfully returned to life?” Lu Mingfei trembled.

“I wasn’t dead. Don’t let the students’ little game frighten you. It’s just live-action Counter-Strike. Today is Freedom Day. Students can do what they like without punishment under college rules.” He sat beside Lu Mingfei.
“But you’re covered in blood!”
“Oh, a tiny piece of alchemical equipment. Frigga rounds. They use them as toys.” He took a cartridge from his pocket. Its bullet was an eerie deep red.

“In Norse mythology, Frigga is Odin’s wife. To protect her son Baldr, god of light, she made everything in the world swear not to harm him. Everything swore, so even spears thrown at him would veer away. When these alchemical bullets hit, they instantly fragment and vaporize. No injury, just a bloodlike stain. They contain a trace anesthetic that immediately knocks you out. Originally tranquilizer rounds, now a Freedom Day tradition. Watch.” He jabbed the bullet hard against the back of his hand. The solid projectile burst into blood-red dust, like the spray from a gunshot wound.
“That… that advanced?” Lu Mingfei marveled.
The professor’s face twitched, and he toppled at Lu Mingfei’s feet.
“Did… returning to life fail?” Lu Mingfei’s face twitched, too.
“Idiot. The anesthetic took effect. Same as getting shot again.” Manstein frowned. “Nurse! Another injection for him!”

The corpse-strewn battlefield now bustled like a sports meet. Medics injected the fallen one by one, then massaged shoulders and backs of the “dead” who had twisted joints while fainting, recording student numbers as they went. Once unmasked, the corpses were all eighteen- or nineteen-year-olds. The first thing they did on waking was whisper about who had won. Nobody quite knew. Both leaders lay in the parking lot, Caesar’s head on Chu’s arm and Chu’s on Caesar’s thigh, unusually intimate, huge bloodstains on their chests. Murasame and Dictator lay nearby.
Apparently someone had shot the two rivals while they dueled.
“Who did it?” someone yelled.
Lu Mingfei sat stiff-faced on the steps, wearing an expression that said INNOCENT PASSERBY.
“Quiet! More trouble? You’ve gone too far this year!” Manstein shouted. “You violated Freedom Day’s special rules. I’ll report this to the principal and have it canceled!”
“The three special rules: no alchemical equipment from the Ice Cellar, no casualties, no outside visitors. Correct?” someone asked.
“They only hurt themselves falling over. Everyone falls, don’t they?” another said.

The speakers were Caesar and Chu. Newly awake, the sworn enemies were calm as captains returning from a soccer match. Each leaned against one side of the passage, arms folded almost identically. Caesar was languid; Chu expressionless.

“Fine! Caesar! Chu Zihang! You’ve got nerve! Wait until I tell the principal!” Manstein’s hands shook with anger as he took out his phone and dialed. Everyone quieted. The principal evidently held an exceptional place in their minds. Every eye fixed on the phone.
Looking like a man wielding supreme authority, Manstein stabbed the speakerphone button.
“Hello, Manstein.” The low, cultured voice sounded like that of a perfect European gentleman, yet the Chinese was impeccable.

“Principal Anjou, forgive the interruption. An exceptional situation. Students are suspected of violating this year’s Freedom Day rules. Lionheart and Student Council members used Frigga rounds and turned the entire campus into a battlefield. Many injuries… substantial property damage. Extremely serious!” Manstein spoke with righteous severity. “And our proud students, especially Lionheart president Chu Zihang and Student Council president Caesar Gattuso, show no respect whatsoever for the Disciplinary Committee.”
“Oh, Caesar’s always been like that. You should be used to it by now, Manstein,” the principal said mildly.

Manstein hesitated. “There’s also the enormous expense… Preliminary repair estimates are around two hundred forty thousand dollars… Not including replacing the lawn. They’ve trampled your favorite Bermuda grass into a field ready for plowing!”
“Caesar, as our wealthiest student, you wouldn’t mind paying to replace my beloved Bermuda grass?” the principal asked.
“As you please.” Caesar shrugged. His Chinese was fluent enough for idiomatic phrases.

“Never mind. I’m joking. Take it from the board’s fund. After all, the students won their annual anniversary celebration, Freedom Day, from us through their own efforts. We old fellows won’t go back on our word.” He laughed warmly. “Enjoy your holiday, then apply yourselves to your studies, my dear students. I wish I could spend this happy Freedom Day with you.”
They exchanged glances and applauded together. Cheering, they untied their armbands and tossed them up, draped arms across one another’s shoulders, swayed, and pulled teasing faces at Manstein.

Lu Mingfei applauded, too, beaming and nodding around to say, Hey, I’m one of you. I’m happy you’re making fun of the bald old guy, too. As a newcomer, he rapidly grasped his position. To survive here, he couldn’t be seen as the class officer who reported everyone to teachers. Public enemy of the students was a death sentence.
“There’s someone else I’d like to greet,” the principal said loudly.
Everyone paused. Silence returned.
“Is our S-rank freshman Lu Mingfei there? Chosen your courses? Did you choose my Introduction to Dragon Genealogy?” His voice echoed around them.
Astonishment filled their eyes. Whispers broke out everywhere.
“I did… I think… I chose it,” Lu Mingfei said timidly. He had to answer. Guderian had taken the phone from Manstein and placed it before him.
“Delighted to hear your voice. Taking down Caesar and Chu on your first day! I look forward to meeting you in class. Do even better than your S-rank predecessor!” The principal hung up.

Lu Mingfei scratched his head. Better how? How could he surpass a senior who had shot himself over philosophy? Kill himself with an aircraft cannon? Suddenly, the temperature seemed to drop. Looking around, he found every eye fixed on him, cold with hostility.
Sunlight slanted through a porthole. The man in shadow ended the call, leaned back, and exhaled silently. Beyond the window lay a river. Their boat was passing between two mountains.

“Caesar and Chu causing trouble again?” the middle-aged man opposite asked. “Freedom Day repairs cost more every year. Perhaps we should limit it. Geniuses may enjoy unrestrained lives, but they’re supposed to be disciplined soldiers.”
“I deliberately give them room. Ten years ago, Cassell was a mysterious military fortress. But Mans, remember our defeat ten years ago?”
He nodded and sipped his black tea. “No one could forget.”
“A well-trained army, annihilated. I had to rethink our educational approach. Perhaps in the war against dragons we need geniuses, not armies.” The principal switched to English. “Somebody.”
“Somebody?”
“The One! A unique genius. A leader. A dragon slayer even Dragon Kings fear. One would be enough. Like my friend Meinhard Cassell.” He spoke quietly. “Genius needs freedom to grow.”
“Perhaps. Caesar and Chu are unprecedented talents. But Lu Mingfei… You rated him S.” The middle-aged man frowned. “I deliberately delayed the CC1000 to extend his observation period. But…”
“He’s too ordinary?” The principal smiled.
“I see nothing exceptional.”

“Don’t be too surprised, but I don’t know him well enough either. I don’t know what he can do. His S-rank has a reason, though I can’t tell you yet,” the principal said. “He may be the genius we await. Or utterly useless.”
“Put someone useless between the tremendous forces of Caesar and Chu, and he’ll be crushed.”

The principal scratched his graying hair. “Too early to call him useless.” He rose and looked outside. It was flood season. Little white flowers bloomed in the dark-green turf on the river islands along both shores.

“We’re passing above Kuimen. Before the Three Gorges Reservoir, the mountains on either side stood like gateposts,” he said softly. “The ancient Chinese spoke of the kui dragon, an ancient one-legged creature. Does Kuimen mean they once saw a dragon swimming here? When does Operation Kuimen begin?”
“In a week. Ye Sheng and Aki are ready. They’re my finest people. With the modified Moniach, I’m confident.”
“If our suspicions are right, don’t wake it. The King of Bronze and Fire, a noble first-generation dragon. No one can guess his power,” the principal said. “Come back safely.”
Late at night, Lu Mingfei sat cross-legged on his bunk, staring out the window.
He had been assigned Room 303 in Dormitory Area One, sharing with Fingel. When he had entered, head hanging, Fingel had been snoring on the upper bunk, utterly unaffected by the gunfire.
“You all right?” Fingel poked his head down.
“You don’t know what happened today.” Lu Mingfei sighed.
“I do. Your heroic exploits are sung across campus. You’re on the college news site. Quite a headline.” Fingel lowered his laptop for him to see.
“Who Claims the Freedom Day Crown? Who Blew Away Caesar, Then Chu Zihang?”
Below was a huge photograph of Lu Mingfei, with his student number, room, age, hometown, and every other detail. The final item kindly specified: SINGLE!
“Looks like a lonely-hearts ad…” he said.
“A wanted poster!” Fingel said. “You still don’t understand what you’ve done.”
“I didn’t do anything. I got a little worked up. Bullets everywhere. Wouldn’t you defend yourself?”

“Self-defense is fine. Blowing away Caesar and Chu with two shots when they only had blades—is that self-defense? And understand this: you won Freedom Day. You’d completed enrollment, so you were a student and eligible. You entered as a third side and were the last survivor. You won!”
“Prize money?”

“Far better. First, a year’s use of Norton Hall! Second, automatic qualification for next year’s Campus Star finals! And finally…” Fingel sounded awed. “The first girl you pursue here can’t turn you down and has to stay with you at least three months!”
“I have a very bad feeling…” Lu Mingfei grew wary.
“Understand why every guy here hates you now? Move the mouse over your picture.”
A blood-red cross appeared, plainly labeled: LOOK CLOSELY! THIS IS THE SON OF A BITCH! WHO’S GOING TO KILL HIM?
He turned completely to stone.
Bang, bang. A knock made him jump like a rabbit.
“Easy, easy. Nobody’s breaking in for revenge. They’ll show me some respect.” Fingel jumped down to open it.
Professor Guderian entered, delighted. His first act was a hearty shoulder-thumping. “Hey, my boy! I’m proud of you! Your name’s everywhere on campus in a single day!”
“Blow up the Pentagon and your name’ll be everywhere in America in a day, too…”
“What brings you here so late?” Fingel asked.
The professor handed Lu Mingfei an envelope. “Your student ID. This card gives you S-rank privileges throughout campus. Also, tomorrow’s the 3E exam. Are you ready?”
“The 3E exam?” Lu Mingfei stared. “What 3E exam?”
“A little test. Others might find it troublesome. For an S-rank like you, easy.”
“On what? Standardized? Just multiple choice and true or false?”
“Only Draconic. The dragons’ spoken and written language,” the professor said casually.
Lu Mingfei nearly lost his breath. “You said languages could be waived! What Draconic? Dragons write? How could anything like that exist?”

“Draconic isn’t foreign. It’s one of your native languages. You have dragon blood,” the professor said. “No need to study. It’s memory inherited through your bloodline. You’re S-rank. Your dragon blood is amazingly pure. You’ll understand naturally when you see it.”
He set both hands on Lu Mingfei’s shoulders and looked into his eyes. “Mingfei. Concentrate. Listen to every sound!”
Unfamiliar retroflex sounds burst from his mouth. An unimaginable way of speaking: thick and hoarse, yet carrying a sovereign’s authority, like church bells.
Lu Mingfei froze, staring at the ceiling, sadness appearing on his face.
“Praise our king’s awakening. Destruction is rebirth,” the professor translated. “Mingfei, did you hear the ancient Dragon Emperor’s voice? I can tell by your face. You understood!”
He turned to Fingel. “See? S-rank ability. Even when you were A-rank, you weren’t this sensitive to Draconic.”
Fingel waved a hand before Lu Mingfei’s vacant eyes. “Whoa. Looks like a mental shock. Spirit vision? Draconic characters appearing in your mind?”

“Understood, my ass. You’ve made a mistake… I really tried, but I still don’t understand!” Lu Mingfei looked miserable. “Are you sure you recruited the right person? There’s more than one Lu Mingfei in China.”
“You… didn’t understand?” The professor stared. “Then why do you look so sad?”
“Of course I’m sad. If I can’t understand it, I can’t pass.”
“Impossible… No visions at all? No feeling of… a great sovereign calling you?” The professor was badly shaken.
“I thought you were singing…” Lu Mingfei said cautiously.
After a brief fit of agitation, Guderian abruptly regained scholarly composure. Grasping his shoulders, he declared, “The first case! The very first! Interesting! Fascinating!”
“First case of what?” Fingel asked.
“The first dragon-blood descendant not to respond to the Dragon Emperor’s call!” He studied Lu Mingfei like a precious specimen. “You’ve mutated!”
“You’ve gone nuts,” Lu Mingfei said.

“Listen. Awe of Draconic is inherited through dragon blood. Every hybrid responds to Yanling: Emperor. But you’ve undergone a genetic mutation and become insensitive. You’re unique!” The old man was excited. “Is this why you’re rated S?”
“Wait! Another possibility: I’m an ordinary human. Right?” Lu Mingfei said. “Doesn’t that explanation make far more sense?”

“Impossible! The principal never misjudges bloodlines.” Guderian rubbed his hands. “You must be extraordinary!” Then his face fell. “But what about tomorrow’s exam? Who besides me will believe it’s a mutation rather than a weak bloodline?”
“I will!” Fingel raised his hand. “You can tell he’s mutated just by his face!”
“A problem. This could affect my tenure review.” Guderian scratched his head.
“Tenure review? What’s that got to do with it?”

“Well, I don’t have tenure here yet.” The old man looked embarrassed. “I’ve been here over ten years and I’m still an assistant professor. The principal did me a favor, assigning you to me. An unprecedented S-rank, he said, with unmatched potential. Training you into an excellent student would be as easy as the New York Yankees winning next year’s Major League Baseball championship. Then I could get tenure.”
“What is all this? Didn’t you say you used to be a Harvard professor?”
“Yes. But to go from Harvard tenure to Cassell tenure, you must successfully train a student.”
Lu Mingfei’s vision darkened. “So… I’m an S-rank student with an assistant professor who has no teaching experience as my adviser?”
“Not quite. I did have one student after coming here. His name is Fingel…” He patted the man beside him, whose face said NOTHING TO DO WITH ME.
“Oh… So that’s why I’m sharing a room with this extraordinary specimen?” Lu Mingfei understood.

“I understand your despair. But face reality.” Fingel sighed. “You’re in a useless professor’s group, with a useless senior who hasn’t graduated in eight years. Every male student wants your head. And I have the saddest news of all.”
“What?” Lu Mingfei thrust out his chest. “Come on! It can’t get worse. I refuse to believe it!”
“That Nono, or Chen Motong, you talked about the whole way…” Fingel leaned close to his ear. “She’s Caesar’s girlfriend!”
“Now I believe it…” Lu Mingfei said. Something deep in his heart gave a faint twitch, then suddenly felt empty.
